name: open()
description: Opens a file by pathname and returns a file descriptor. The kernel resolves the path through the dentry cache, creates or looks up the inode, performs permission checks, allocates a file descriptor, and installs the new struct file into the process's file table.
signature: int open(const char *pathname, int flags, mode_t mode)

main_flow.title: User Space
main_flow.description: The user-space program invokes open("./passwd", O_RDONLY) via the C library wrapper (glibc), which places the syscall number (NR_open = 2 on x86-64) in %rax and the arguments in %rdi, %rsi, %rdx, then executes the syscall instruction to trap into the kernel.

detail_nodes.title: glibc open() wrapper
detail_nodes.description: The GNU C Library provides a thin wrapper around the raw syscall. It sets up the ABI-defined calling convention: %rax = __NR_open (2), %rdi = pathname pointer, %rsi = flags, %rdx = mode. No kernel involvement yet — this is pure user-space setup.

detail_nodes.title: syscall instruction
detail_nodes.description: The syscall instruction atomically saves %rip and %rflags into MSR_LSTAR-defined kernel entry, switches to ring 0, and loads the kernel stack pointer from the TSS. Control jumps to the system_call entry point in entry_64.S.

source_ref.snippet:
ENTRY(system_call)
  SWAPGS_UNSAFE_STACK
  movq %rsp, PER_CPU_VAR(old_rsp)
  movq PER_CPU_VAR(kernel_stack),%rsp

detail_nodes.title: Pathname in user memory
detail_nodes.description: The pathname string (e.g., "./passwd") resides in the user-space process's address space. The kernel must copy it into kernel space during path lookup to safely traverse the filesystem. The getname() helper performs this copy and checks for valid path characters.

main_flow.title: Kernel Entry
main_flow.description: The CPU is now in ring 0. The generic syscall dispatch table routes NR_open to sys_open(), which calls do_sys_open(). The kernel copies the pathname from user space, then begins the process of opening the file.

detail_nodes.title: system_call entry point
detail_nodes.description: entry_64.S saves all general-purpose registers, re-enables interrupts, then calls sys_call_table[%rax] to dispatch to the correct syscall handler. For NR_open (2), this calls sys_open().

detail_nodes.title: SYSCALL_DEFINE3(open, ...)
detail_nodes.description: sys_open() is defined with the SYSCALL_DEFINE3 macro in fs/open.c. It calls do_sys_open(), passing the flags, mode, and a temporary kernel-space copy of the pathname obtained via getname().

detail_nodes.title: do_sys_open()
detail_nodes.description: do_sys_open() is the central open dispatcher. It calls get_unused_fd_flags() to reserve a file descriptor slot, then calls do_filp_open() to create and initialize the struct file. Finally it calls fd_install() to bind the fd to the file in the process's file table.

main_flow.title: Path Lookup
main_flow.description: The kernel resolves the pathname by walking each component ("./" → "passwd") through the filesystem hierarchy. Starting from the current working directory's dentry, it follows each path segment, checking mount points and symbolic links along the way.

detail_nodes.title: do_path_lookup()
detail_nodes.description: do_path_lookup() is the main pathname resolution engine. It initializes a nameidata struct with the starting dentry (current->fs->pwd.dentry), then calls link_path_walk() to iterate over each path component.

detail_nodes.title: link_path_walk()
detail_nodes.description: link_path_walk() iterates over each path component separated by '/'. For each component it calls do_lookup() to resolve the name in the current directory, handling '.' (current dir), '..' (parent dir), and regular names.

detail_nodes.title: struct nameidata
detail_nodes.description: nameidata is the central state structure for pathname resolution. It tracks the current path (dentry + vfsmount), the last component's name, the lookup intent (create, open, etc.), and symlink recursion depth.

main_flow.title: Dentry Cache
main_flow.description: For each path component, the kernel first checks the dentry cache (dcache) to see if the component has been looked up before. A cache hit avoids expensive filesystem operations. On a miss, a new dentry is allocated and linked into the cache.

detail_nodes.title: d_lookup()
detail_nodes.description: d_lookup() searches the dentry hash table for a matching name under the parent dentry. The hash is computed from the parent pointer and the component name. On a hit, the existing dentry is returned with its reference count incremented.

detail_nodes.title: d_alloc() — cache miss
detail_nodes.description: On a cache miss, d_alloc() creates a new dentry structure. It allocates memory from the dentry slab cache, initializes the d_name field with the component name, and links the new dentry into the parent's d_subdirs list.

detail_nodes.title: struct dentry
detail_nodes.description: struct dentry represents a directory entry in the VFS namespace. It caches the name-to-inode mapping, avoiding repeated filesystem lookups. Key fields include d_inode (the inode pointer), d_parent (parent dentry), d_subdirs (children list), and d_op (dentry operations like d_revalidate).

main_flow.title: Inode & Permission
main_flow.description: Once the final dentry is resolved, the kernel retrieves or creates the inode (via the filesystem's lookup or iget_locked). It then performs permission checks: filesystem-level ACLs, SELinux/AppArmor MAC checks, and standard Unix permission bits (rwx) against the process's UID/GID.

detail_nodes.title: iget_locked()
detail_nodes.description: iget_locked() looks up an inode in the inode cache by superblock and inode number. If not found, it allocates a new inode from the filesystem's inode slab, initializes it, and inserts it into the inode hash table. The filesystem then fills in the inode via its read_inode method.

detail_nodes.title: may_open()
detail_nodes.description: may_open() is the core permission validation for open(). It checks that the requested access mode (read/write) is compatible with the file's type and permissions, verifies the inode's UID/GID against the process's credentials, and enforces mandatory access control (MAC) policies.

detail_nodes.title: inode_permission()
detail_nodes.description: inode_permission() performs the standard Unix permission check: it compares the file's mode bits (owner/group/other rwx) against the process's effective UID and GID, following the CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE capability rules for privileged processes.

main_flow.title: FD Allocation
main_flow.description: With the inode validated and permissions granted, the kernel allocates a file descriptor and creates a struct file to represent the open file. The file descriptor is installed into the process's file descriptor table, making it visible to user space.

detail_nodes.title: get_unused_fd_flags()
detail_nodes.description: get_unused_fd_flags() searches the process's fdtable for the lowest unused file descriptor number. It starts from current->files->next_fd as a hint for efficiency. If the fdtable is full, it expands the array.

detail_nodes.title: nameidata_to_filp()
detail_nodes.description: nameidata_to_filp() creates a new struct file from the resolved nameidata. It calls dentry_open() to allocate the file structure, sets up the file operations (f_op) from the inode, initializes the file position to 0, and applies any O_ flags (O_APPEND, O_NONBLOCK, etc.).

detail_nodes.title: fd_install()
detail_nodes.description: fd_install() binds the allocated file descriptor number to the struct file pointer in the process's fdtable. After this call, user space can use the fd integer to refer to this open file in subsequent syscalls like read(), write(), and close().

main_flow.title: Return Path
main_flow.description: sys_open() returns the newly allocated file descriptor number (a small non-negative integer) to user space. The C library wrapper receives it in %rax and returns it to the caller. On error, a negative errno (e.g., -ENOENT, -EACCES) is returned instead.

detail_nodes.title: do_sys_open() returns fd
detail_nodes.description: do_sys_open() returns the allocated fd to sys_open(), which returns it through the syscall dispatch. If any step failed (path not found, permission denied, too many open files), the error code propagates back instead.

detail_nodes.title: Syscall return — sysret
detail_nodes.description: sys_open() returns the fd (or negative errno) to the syscall dispatch in entry_64.S. The RESTORE_ARGS macro reloads the saved user-space registers, and the sysretq instruction atomically restores %rip, %rflags, and switches back to ring 3. The C library wrapper receives the return value in %rax.

source_ref.snippet:
sysret_check:
  LOCKDEP_SYS_EXIT
  DISABLE_INTERRUPTS(CLBR_NONE)
  movl %_TIF_ALLWORK_MASK,%edi
  andl %edi,%edx
  jnz sysret_careful
  RESTORE_ARGS 0,-ARG_SKIP,0
  movq PER_CPU_VAR(old_rsp), %rsp
  USERGS_SYSRET64

detail_nodes.title: User space receives fd
detail_nodes.description: The user program receives the file descriptor (e.g., fd = 3) as the return value of open(). It can now use this fd in subsequent system calls. The kernel has created all necessary data structures (struct file, dentry, inode reference) that will persist until close() is called.
